title: Continuous fabrication of Janus liquid crystal elastomer fibers with programmable actuation

paper_content.abstract: Smart fibers, particularly liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) fibers, are pivotal in soft robotics and adaptive textiles. However, existing fabrication methods are limited to simple monolithic structures, hindering the realization of complex actuation behaviors. To overcome this limitation, we develop a continuous extrusion platform for producing Janus LCE fibers that emulate asymmetric biological structures, such as plant tendrils, thereby enabling sophisticated actuation. This approach seamlessly integrates an LCE network with a dynamic covalent polymer network, allowing programmable on-demand liquid crystal orientation for actuation via dynamic bond exchange. The resulting Janus fibers exhibit enhanced mechanical properties and multifunctional capabilities, including adaptive object manipulation, stimuli-responsive directional motion, and scalable integration into smart fabrics for thermal management. By unifying material intelligence with structural programmability, this work advances the development of bioinspired soft robotic systems with enhanced environmental adaptability.
paper_content.introduction:
Fibrous artificial muscles 1–6 are crucial for a wide range of applications, including prosthetic limbs 6, adaptive textiles 7–10, and miniature actuators 5, 11–14. Among polymer-based smart fibers (e.g., responsive gels 15, 16, shape-memory polymers 17, 18, dielectric elastomers 19, and thermally expandable polymers), liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) stand out due to their high reversible strain and rapid response 20. Their actuation behavior is determined by two key factors: geometric structure and liquid crystal orientation, where the former dictates their application scenarios and the latter governs their ability to undergo reversible deformation under external stimuli. Building on the seminal study that established the basic principle for producing LCE fibers via mechanical stretching followed by photopolymerization to achieve mesogen alignment 21, several advanced fabrication techniques have emerged. These include melt drawing 22, direct ink writing 23, 24, and electrospinning 25, 26, all proven effective in fabricating LCE fibers with strong actuation properties. Their structures, however, are typically constrained to simple and monolithic forms, which limits the potential for achieving complex actuation behaviors.

In nature, plants like tendrils exhibit sophisticated deformations through asymmetric fiber lignification, forming helical structures that are capable of multimodal bending and coiling, thereby adapting to the environment 27. Mimicking such mechanisms in artificial muscles requires replicating intrinsic structural complexity, yet existing approaches struggle to achieve this. Pioneering work demonstrating “self-winding” LCE utilized a mold-fabricated helical precursor. Locking the orientation during secondary stretching enabled controllable shape transformations, including bending, twisting, coiling, and contraction, within a monolithic fibrous architecture 28. An elegant approach involves leveraging the shear gradient differential between the core and sheath during direct ink writing to program varying liquid crystal orientations in LCE fibers, enabling complex actuation modalities 29. This approach primarily modulates orientation distributions while remaining constrained in terms of hierarchical structural design.

Janus architectures, integrating two distinct materials with different functionalities within a compact structure, offer an innovative paradigm for sophisticated structural and functional design 30–32. Fabricating Janus architectures beyond nanoparticles or thin membranes remains challenging, primarily due to the difficulty in achieving uniform anisotropic construction throughout three-dimensional fibrous structures. Although millimeter-scale Janus hydrogel fibers have been produced via wet spinning 33, these methodologies prove fundamentally incompatible with LCE. This arises from LCEs’ stringent requirements for both liquid crystal phase preservation and precise liquid crystal orientation, a criterion that current hydrogel-based fabrication techniques cannot meet due to inherent chemical constraints. Furthermore, these existing approaches are restricted to producing large-diameter fibers, limiting their applicability. We envision whether we can fabricate a Janus fiber that combines asymmetric structural design with multifunctional performance. The selection of material composition is critical: one component should provide actuation capabilities, while the other serves as a structural support with programmable orientation control. Here, dynamic covalent polymers 34–36, usually copolymerized with LCE, are particularly well-suited for this purpose, as their bond exchange reactions permit the on-demand programming of liquid crystal orientation. Beyond that, dynamic covalent polymers like polyurethane enhance mechanical robustness significantly when incorporated into LCE to form interpenetrating networks, enabling ultrastrong actuation-mechanics properties and representing a milestone in high-performance LCE development 37.

Therefore, we present in this work a continuous asymmetric extrusion platform for the seamless integration of an LCE network (for actuation) with a dynamic covalent polymer network (for programming). The selection of compatible chemistries is critical, as the two polymer precursors must exhibit matched extrusion viscosities, identical curing conditions, and synchronized curing kinetics. Through precise chemical design, we employ UV-curable LCE and the dynamic covalent polymer to enable continuous Janus fiber production. The resulting Janus fibers exhibit adaptive object manipulation, directional motion under thermal/infrared laser stimuli, and navigation capabilities in complex environments. This work merges material intelligence with structural programmability, paving the way for multifunctional soft robots with bioinspired environmental adaptability.
paper_content.results:
Bioinspired continuous fabrication of Janus fibers
As Fig. 1a illustrates, plant tendrils usually induce anisotropic contraction through asymmetric lignification of gelatinous fiber (g-fiber) cells, which finally leads to helical coiling to adapt to the environment 27. Such tendrils can be considered as natural Janus structures capable of switching between “on” and “off” states through the modulation of intrinsic curvature 38. This characteristic enables them to be sufficiently compliant for interaction with the environment while remaining mechanically robust enough to perform functional tasks (Fig. 1b). Inspired by this, we design a continuous asymmetric spinning platform to fabricate Janus fibers (Fig. 1c and Movie S1). This platform co-extrudes two precursors through a conical Janus nozzle, followed by an in situ ultraviolet (UV) light curing. These two precursors are composed of LCE and polyurethane (PU) precursors, respectively (Fig. 1d). Specifically, the LCE precursor is synthesized via the thiol-Michael addition reaction among 1,4-bis[4-(6-acryloyloxyhexyloxy)benzoyloxy]-2-methylbenzene (RM82), 3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol (DODT), and pentaerythritol tetrakis(3-mercaptopropionate) (PETMP). The PU precursor is prepared in accordance with the procedure described in the literature 33. The chemical structures of both precursors are characterized by nuclear magnetic resonance, as shown in Fig. S1. Janus fibers that contained these two materials are then partially cured through the photoinitiated free radical polymerization of (meth)acrylate from two precursors.

To further induce mesogens alignment in LCE, the fibers are mechanically drawn using a differential-speed winding system, followed by a secondary UV curing process, which allows the materials to be fully cured to lock the strain-induced orientation. This dual-step curing process separates geometric structure formation from functional orientation fixing, enabling programmable on-demand actuation of LCE. Subsequent thermal annealing facilitates the ordered reorganization of hydrogen bonds through dynamic bond exchange within the PU segments, ultimately strengthening the mechanical integrity of the fibers 35.

The experimental details of the whole process can be found in the Supplementary Information. All processing steps can be conducted under ambient conditions without the need for oxygen degassing. This facilitates greater accessibility and scalability of the process, while ensuring the maintenance of chemical fidelity. Consequently, the Janus fiber obtained through this method exhibit a well-defined biphasic morphology in cross-section at the microscopic level (Fig. 1e) and possess the potential for scalable production at the macroscopic level (Fig. 1f). Compared with conventional LCE fibers reported in the literature 5, 29, 39–52, it demonstrates not only a higher elastic modulus but also greater breaking strength, which can be attributed to the mechanical reinforcement provided by the PU component (Fig. 1g).

The successful continuous fabrication of Janus fibers relies on achieving precise compatibility in both rheological behavior and polymerization kinetics between the LCE and dynamic covalent PU network. Gel permeation chromatography results reveal that they possess the molecular weight of 1.1 × 10^5 and 4.4 × 10^4 g/mol, respectively (Fig. S2). The stable co-extrusion capability can be attributed to the high viscosity (5500 and 2200 Pa·s) and the shear-thinning behavior of both precursors (Fig. 2a and Fig. S3). In contrast, viscosity mismatch or excessively low viscosities disrupt interfacial stability, leading to distorted Janus interfaces or droplet-like co-extrusion morphologies, underscoring the necessity of maintaining an appropriately matched rheological window for continuous fiber formation (Figs. S4 and S5). More importantly, the photopolymerization kinetics of the two precursors exhibit remarkable synchronization. Upon exposure to 365 nm UV light, the LCE precursor undergoes rapid photopolymerization, as evidenced by time-resolved infrared spectroscopy and the corresponding increase in acrylate conversion (Fig. 2b and Fig. S6). According to Flory’s gelation theory, the LCE precursor reaches the gel point after 2 s of exposure (calculations provided in the Supporting Information). Similarly, the PU precursor displays comparably fast crosslinking kinetics, with the gel fraction exceeding >21% within 2 s (Fig. 2c). These rapid curing dynamics enable the concurrent formation of both networks, thereby ensuring fiber solidification during the initial stages of UV curing.

Properties regulation of Janus fibers
The composition and morphology of Janus fibers can be further regulated by adjusting the extrusion speed. As shown in Fig. 2d, when the extrusion speeds of LCE and PU precursor solutions are identical, the diameter of the Janus fibers decreases with increasing extrusion speed. Conversely, when the extrusion speeds differ, the component with the slower extrusion speed exhibits a higher content (Fig. 2e). Hereafter, we use the same extrusion speed of 5 m·min^−1. Longitudinal SEM images confirm the clear two-phase interface along the fiber axis. SEM images of knotted fibers show that the Janus architecture remains intact under complex deformation, demonstrating structural robustness (Fig. S7). Moreover, two materials in Janus fibers remain unchanged when subjected to different imposed twist levels (Fig. S8), confirming interfacial stability under torsion.

The two-step UV curing strategy enables precise control over the crosslinking density to fix the mesogen orientation during fiber stretching (Fig. S9). To evaluate the mesogen alignment in fully UV-cured LCE, polarized optical microscopy (POM) is used to characterize the orientational order of the LCE phase in Janus fibers. When the fiber axis (i.e., mesogen alignment direction) is parallel to the polarizer, the fiber appears dark. When rotated to 45° relative to the polarizer, one half of the fiber became bright, indicating well-aligned LCE mesogens (Fig. 2f). The degree of fiber orientation is determined by the speed ratio of V3 to V2, as illustrated in Fig. 1c. As shown in Fig. S10, a higher speed ratio corresponds to more pronounced birefringence effects. Two-dimensional wide-angle X-ray scattering (2D-WAXS) shows effective mesogen alignment (Fig. 2g), because the initially isotropic diffraction ring becomes anisotropic arcs perpendicular to the alignment direction. Increasing the stretching speed ratio from 1 to 1.8 induces a rise in the orientational order parameter from 0 to 0.61, as calculated from Fig. S11.

Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) identifies two distinct thermal transitions in the Janus fiber. The first corresponds to the glass transition temperature (Tg) of ~17°C, originating from the soft-segment matrix of the LCE network, while the second represents the nematic-to-isotropic transition temperature (TNI) of around 67°C, characteristic of the mesogenic domains within the LCE (Fig. 2h). The PU network exhibits stress relaxation behavior above 55°C, with a faster relaxation rate observed at higher temperatures. This results in an activation energy of ~54.9 kJ·mol^−1, confirming the efficient dynamic exchange of hydrogen bonds in the PU network (Fig. 2i). Beyond that, the resulting Janus fibers demonstrate excellent mechanical performance. As shown in Fig. S12, the fibers exhibit a tensile strain of 156%, a tensile strength of 40.4 MPa, a Young’s modulus of 12.7 MPa, and a toughness of 17.1 MJ·m^−3. Comparison with pure LCE and PU fibers reveals that the Janus architecture significantly enhances breaking strength, effectively overcoming the mechanical limitations of conventional single-network LCE systems (Fig. 2j). This improvement arises from the synergistic integration of the aligned LCE phase and dynamic covalent PU network. A visual demonstration shows that a single Janus fiber (diameter ~200 μm) is capable of supporting a hanging load exceeding 160,000 times its own weight over a vertical distance of ~20 cm during externally driven motion (Fig. S13 and Movie S2), highlighting the exceptional strength and robustness of this hybrid design. To better understand the factors governing mechanical performance, we examined the effect of extrusion speed. Higher extrusion speeds produce thinner fibers, which exhibit increased Young’s modulus and enhanced toughness, revealing a clear dependence of mechanical properties on fiber diameter that can be systematically tuned through the extrusion parameters (Fig. S14). In addition to their improved mechanical robustness, the continuously extruded Janus fibers also display excellent thermal actuation performance. Upon heating, the fibers undergo a transition from a linear to a helical configuration; therefore, the reported actuation strain corresponds to a length-change ratio rather than a conventional uniaxial contraction strain. The effective fiber length in the helical state was measured as illustrated in Fig. S15, and the detailed calculation formula for the actuation strain is provided in the Supporting Information. At 80°C, the fibers exhibit an actuation strain of ~85%, defined here as the length-change ratio, together with a high actuation strain rate of 193%·s^−1, and generate an energy density approaching 50 kJ·m^−3 under a load of 200 kPa (Figs. S15 and S16). Collectively, these mechanical and actuation characteristics indicate the potential applicability of Janus fibers in scalable artificial-muscle systems (see Table S3 for quantitative comparison).

Programmable and reprogrammable actuation of Janus fibers
The inherent soft elasticity of LCE 53 and the dynamic bond exchange in PU enable various programming strategies for shaping and actuating Janus fibers. The first strategy involves direct mechanical stretching (Fig. 3a i). At room temperature, LCE exhibits soft elasticity and retains its stretched shape after the force is removed (Fig. S17). In contrast, PU shows entropic elasticity and returns to its original shape once the force is released. As a result, the Janus fiber can coil due to the asymmetric contraction of the two materials after mechanical programming. Further heating would remove the soft elasticity of LCE, causing the coiling to disappear. Representative images of the process are shown in Fig. S18. The applied strain affects the helical structure of the fiber, with higher strain leading to tighter and denser helices (Fig. 3a ii). The helical density, therefore, increases nonlinearly, approaching ~5 cm^−1 at 100% prestrain, while the coil diameter decreases and plateaus near 0.1 cm at higher strains (Fig. 3a iii). The pitch likewise decreases with strain, stabilizing at ~0.2 cm (Fig. S19).

Another approach is precisely the opposite. At elevated temperatures (90°C), LCE is capable of recovering its original shape after the removal of an external force, whereas PU, due to stress relaxation resulting from dynamic bond exchange, undergoes plastic deformation and fails to recover (Fig. S20). Fibers are stretched to 60% strain and subsequently annealed at 90°C for varying durations (Fig. 3b i). The annealing time affects the helical structure of the fibers, with longer annealing durations leading to tighter and denser helices (Fig. 3b ii). The helical density, therefore, increases nonlinearly with annealing time, approaching ~6.5 cm^−1 after prolonged annealing, while the coil diameter decreases and plateaus near 0.08 cm (Fig. 3b iii). The pitch likewise decreases with annealing time, stabilizing at ~0.15 cm (Fig. S21). In this case, when the fibers cool to room temperature, the reversible actuations occur due to the orientation of LCE, which will be discussed in detail later.

To further quantify this asymmetry, we introduced a geometric model:
L2 - L1 = N · H · (sqrt(π^2 · D^2 + p^2) - sqrt(π^2 · (D - 2d)^2 + p^2)) (1)
Here, L1 and L2 represent the lengths of the PU and LCE domains, respectively; N is the helical density; H is the axial length of the helix; D is the outer diameter of the helix; d is the diameter of the fiber; and p is the helical pitch (Fig. S22). Substituting experimentally measured parameters into the analytical model revealed distinct trends in the domain length differentials. Under direct mechanical stretching, L2 - L1 was positive and increased with applied strain, reaching a maximum at 100% strain. In contrast, thermal annealing yielded a negative L2 - L1, with the absolute value reaching a maximum after 10 min of annealing, which is in good agreement with experimental results. These observations confirm the effectiveness of the analytical framework in capturing the asymmetric strain-induced coiling behavior of Janus LCE fibers.

Further implementation of spatial programming strategies enables heterogeneous actuation within a single Janus fiber (Fig. 3c). Near-infrared (NIR) laser irradiation (808 nm, 2000 mW·cm^−2, 5 min) is selected to achieve this activation. The fiber is first uniformly stretched to 50% strain under controlled external stress and then selectively irradiated. During programming, even when NIR irradiation raises temperatures above the LCE phase transition, contraction-induced stresses in LCE are insufficient to overcome external stretching, while PU undergoes stress relaxation. Upon release of the applied strain, two distinct regions emerged, exhibiting opposite spiral orientations and differing pitches. Importantly, when heated to 70°C, the irradiated regions transformed into helical structures with varying pitches, while the previously unirradiated region returned to a linear configuration. These results showcase the ability of Janus fibers to achieve programmable, on-demand heterogeneity within a structurally continuous architecture.

Dynamic bonds enable efficient reprogramming of liquid crystal mesogen orientation, allowing the desired actuation (Fig. 4a). Unlike conventional methods that incorporate dynamic bonds into the LCE network through copolymerization 29, 54–56, our Janus design retains efficient reorientation while preserving the strong mechanical properties of dynamic covalent polymers. After programming, the loosely coiled helical configurations are capable of reversibly switching between loose and tight helices and exhibit excellent stability during two hundred heating and cooling cycles (Movie S3), and this reversible actuation is maintained even when small external loads are applied (Fig. S23). Finite element analysis (FEA) is utilized to predict this actuation, and the numerical simulations show close agreement with the experimental results (Fig. 4b). More importantly, these structures can be reprogrammed into diverse helical architectures through dynamic bond exchange (Fig. 4c and Movie S4). Cyclic testing demonstrates that the fibers exhibit no signs of actuation fatigue within 200 cycles (Fig. S24). After 200 actuation cycles, the interfaces of Janus fiber remained intact, demonstrating that fibers produced via our fabrication method exhibit excellent structural stability (Fig. S25). Additional FEA simulations of all three helical structures are conducted (Fig. S26), showing excellent agreement with the experimental results. This characteristic enables the potential application of Janus fibers as soft robots.

Multimodal actuation and functional demonstrations of Janus fiber robots
Inspired by the adaptive grasping mechanism of climbing tendrils, our Janus fibers demonstrate the ability to autonomously coil for object manipulation. Upon approaching a heated wire at 90°C, localized heating induces Janus LCE fiber curling, thereby enabling firm grasping and lifting of the wire (Fig. 5a and Movie S5). Despite a cross-sectional diameter of approximately 170 μm, the fibers are capable of lifting loads up to 0.5 g, corresponding to a load-bearing capacity exceeding 20 N/cm^2. Subsequent cooling allows for the controlled release of the wire. This localized heating can also be achieved through NIR laser irradiation, enabling on-demand light-guided locomotion, with the actuation magnitude precisely tunable via the irradiation intensity (Fig. S27). We therefore design a “water strider”, in which four of its legs are composed of Janus fibers coated with carbon nanotubes. NIR laser irradiation (808 nm, 5000 mW·cm^−2, 0.5 s) of the left-side legs causes the fibers to bend. Removing the light triggers shape recovery, reversing the bending for movement in the opposite direction (Fig. 5b and Movie S6). This “water strider” can achieve an initial average speed of 4.7 mm/s (Fig. S28a). In contrast, NIR laser irradiation (808 nm, 5000 mW·cm^−2, 0.5 s) on the right legs can generate a rotational torque, achieving a controllable clockwise rotation of ~14°/s and reaching an angular displacement of 125° within 9 s (Fig. 5c and Fig. S28b). These results demonstrate that multimodal locomotion can be achieved through the integration of Janus LCE fibers with different actuation directions by leveraging localized NIR laser stimuli. Control experiments employing non-actuating PU fibers as locomotive elements exclude thermally induced Marangoni effects. These results confirm that motion originates from programmed NIR-triggered bending of Janus fibers. The asymmetric leg configuration, in which the left legs have opposite LCE-facing orientations while the right legs share the same orientation, allows selective illumination to generate either a net propulsive force for translation or an unbalanced torque for rotation, enabling the robot to switch between straight-line motion and controlled rotation in a programmable manner.

Heterogeneous structural design of Janus LCE fibers can also enable directional locomotion. To achieve this, we design a spring fiber with gradient helical architectures (Fig. S29). Upon insertion into narrow glass tubes and heating to 100°C, asymmetric contraction along the fiber generates axial movement. During the cooling phase to 40°C, shape recovery further enhances the overall movement. Through repeated thermal cycling, an inchworm-like locomotion is achieved (Fig. 5d and Movie S7), with each cycle resulting in ~0.2 mm of forward progression (Fig. S30).

The continuously fabricated fibers can be incorporated into smart fabrics through conventional textile manufacturing techniques. During the weaving process, Janus LCE fibers are integrated as weft threads in a plain weave structure, enabling active functional control while maintaining mechanical integrity. The resulting textiles display a uniform weave free of defects, confirming the fibers’ robustness under the shear and tensile stresses experienced during the weaving process (Fig. 5e). When stretched, the mechanical stretching induces a structural transformation in the Janus LCE fibers, generating coiled architectures that increase fabric porosity and loft density. This geometric reconfiguration significantly enhances thermal insulation performance, as demonstrated in Fig. 5f and Fig. S31. And the mechanically induced thermal insulation enhancement is reversible, as mild heating initiates structural recovery to the original compact form. The highly tunable insulation properties render the material exceptionally suitable for wearable and adaptive thermal management applications.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
1,4-Bis [4-(6-acryloyloxyhexyloxy)benzoyloxy]-2-methylbenzene (RM82) was procured from Daken Chemical Company. 3,6-Dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol (DODT, 97%), Tolylene-2,4-diisocyanate (95%) and 2-(tert-butylamino)ethyl methacrylate (98%) was obtained from TCI. Pentaerythritol tetrakis (3-mercaptopropionate) (PETMP, 95%), triethylamine (TEA, 99%), dimethylolbutanoic acid (DMBA, 98%), ditin butyl dilaurate (DBTDL, 95%), and Phenylbis(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl) phosphine oxide (Irgacure 819, 97%) were obtained from Aladdin. Poly(tetrahydrofuran)diol (Mn=1000) was purchased from B&D and vacuum-dried at 100°C before being used. All chemicals were used as received unless otherwise noted.

Synthesis of LC oligomer
RM82 (10.00 g), DODT (2.024 g), TEA (2% of the monomers), and toluene (10.00 g) were added into a 50 mL flask and stirred at 70°C for 24 h. After the reaction, toluene was evaporated at 70°C to yield a white viscous liquid, which was further dried in a 70°C vacuum oven for 24 h. The molecular structure was characterized by 1H-NMR and FTIR analysis (Figs. S1a and S4).

Synthesis of PU precursor
The PU precursor containing dynamic hindered urea bonds and pendant carboxylic acid groups was synthesized via three steps. First, poly(tetrahydrofuran)diol (0.05 mol) and tolylene-2,4-diisocyanate (0.1 mol) were added to a three-necked flask equipped with a mechanical stirrer, followed by the addition of the catalyst DBTDL (0.1 wt% of poly(tetrahydrofuran)diol), and stirred at 50°C for 4 h. Subsequently, dimethylolbutanoic acid (0.033 mol) was added and reacted for 4 h. Finally, 2-(tert-butylamino)ethyl methacrylate (0.033 mol) was introduced and reacted for an additional 4 h using ethylene glycol diacetate as the solvent to control viscosity. The molar ratio of dimethylolbutanoic acid to 2-(tert-butylamino)ethyl methacrylate was maintained at 1:1 to ensure equimolar content of hindered urea bonds and carboxylic acid groups. The chemical structure of the resulting PU precursor was confirmed by 1H NMR analysis (Fig. S1b).

Preparation of LCE precursor
Combine LC oligomer (1.00 g), RM82 (0.50 g), DODT (65.20 mg), PETMP (187.30 mg), and Irgacure 819 (10 mg) in toluene (500 μL) with a magnetic stirrer. Stir the solution at room temperature for 30 min to dissolve. The final precursor was collected as a viscous liquid after evaporating the toluene under vacuum. The precursor was ready for use.

Preparation of PU precursor
The PU precursor was mixed with ethylene glycol diacetate for viscosity control, using a maximum solvent content of 40 wt%, followed by the addition of the Irgacure 819 (3 wt%). The resulting mixture was stored in the dark prior to use.

Fabrication system
Janus fibers were fabricated using a custom-built high-speed extrusion-spinning setup comprising a coaxial fiber extrusion module and a synchronized fiber collection unit. The extrusion module employed a modified direct ink writing printhead from a commercial bioprinter (Regenovo, Bio-Printer SR, China) to simultaneously extrude LCE and PU precursors through a custom-designed Janus nozzle under in situ UV irradiation (365 nm, 9000 mW·cm^−2), thereby forming a single biphasic filament. The extrusion and collection speeds were precisely matched to ensure uniform fiber formation. The fiber diameter and the interfacial ratio between the LCE and PU domains were tuned by adjusting the applied air pressure, nozzle diameter, and roller speed. A differential speed between the two rollers (defined by the ratio of V3 to V2) enabled uniaxial stretching of the extruded fiber and was followed by secondary UV curing (365 nm, 9000 mW·cm^−2, 10 min) to achieve further crosslinking of the Janus architecture and to lock in the aligned mesogen orientation within the LCE domain. Unless otherwise specified, the subsequent Janus fibers were fabricated under optimized conditions with an extrusion speed of 5 m·min^−1 and roller speeds set to V1=V2=2 r·min^−1 and V3=V4=3.6 r·min^−1. The Janus nozzle was independently designed and fabricated via DLP 3D printing with a nozzle diameter of 0.4 mm.

Characterization
NIR laser (808 nm) was generated by a laser source (MDL-H-808-5W, Changchun New Industries Optoelectronics Technology Co., Ltd.). Supporting Information Videos were recorded by a digital camera (Sony, Alpha 7). Surface morphology was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-4800). The 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR) spectra were collected on a Bruker Avance III spectrometer operating at 500 MHz. FTIR spectra were recorded using a VERTEX 70 FTIR spectrometer. Gel permeation chromatography (Waters) was performed using tetrahydrofuran as the mobile phase with a flow rate of 1 mL·min^−1. Rheological measurements were conducted with a rotational rheometer (DHR-2, TA Instruments). The alignment and Janus structure of fibers was observed using polarized optical microscopy (POM, ECLIPSE E600W POL) with crossed polarizers. Two-dimensional wide-angle X-ray scattering (2D-WAXS) patterns and data were gathered utilizing an X-ray diffractometer (XENOCS) at room temperature. Mechanical tensile tests of Janus fibers were carried out on a universal testing machine (Instron 5966) at a stretching rate of 20 mm·min^−1. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) was conducted using a TA Q800 analyzer.

Programming strategy 1: direct mechanical stretching
Janus fibers were programmed by subjecting them to tensile strains ranging from 20 to 100% at a temperature of 25°C, followed by the release of the applied strain. The deformed shape was retained due to the soft elasticity exhibited by LCE. The degree of coiling (N) was quantified as the number of coils per unit fiber length (N=n/H), where “H” denotes the original length of the unprogrammed fiber and “n” is the number of visible coils formed after programming. In addition, the coil diameter and helix pitch was measured to assess the morphological response of the fibers under different programming strains.

Programming strategy 2: thermal annealing
Janus fibers were programmed by applying a tensile strain of 60% at 90°C and subsequently annealed for varying durations (1-10 min) under the same temperature, followed by immediate strain release. The resulting deformed shape was attributed to stress relaxation caused by dynamic bond exchange in PU. The resulting coiled configurations were then evaluated as a function of annealing time, and the coil density (N), coil diameter, and helical pitch were further quantified and compared across different annealing times.

Programming strategy 3: spatial programming
Janus fibers were first stretched to 50% strain at 25°C. Near-infrared (808 nm) laser irradiation (2000 mW·cm^−2, 5 min) was then applied in a spatially selective manner to predefined regions along the fiber. The laser was scanned longitudinally along the fiber axis at a controlled speed to locally activate dynamic covalent bond exchange. No observable contraction was detected during programming, indicating that the non-oriented LCE domains and applied external stress prevented deformation gradients, preserving the programming of the PU phase. Upon releasing the applied strain, the laser-irradiated regions—designated as Programming 2—retained their elongated shape, while the non-irradiated regions (Programming 1) spontaneously relaxed into helical coils. This spatially patterned programming yielded a single fiber comprising both linear and helical segments. When heated to 70°C, the fiber exhibited thermally induced bimodal switching: the initially linear segments (Programming 2) transformed into helices, while the preformed helical segments (Programming 1) relaxed into linear configurations. This dual-mode integration highlights a programmable and reversible strategy for spatially encoded multimodal actuation within a single Janus fiber.

Shape reconfiguration of coiling and reversible actuation performance of Janus fibers
Fibers were twisted to a twist density of 6 turns·cm^−1 and heated to ~90°C to activate dynamic bond exchange while introducing internal stress, followed by cooling to ~25°C under constant tension and subsequent release of the applied stress. The resulting fibers were then immersed in oil baths maintained at ~90°C to induce thermally triggered coiling. Simultaneously, further dynamic bond exchange reconfigured and fixed the transient helical shape into a stable geometry. Notably, by varying the inserted twist densities (e.g., 5, 8, and 10 turns·cm^−1), three additional reconfigured helical architectures were generated, each exhibiting distinct geometries and actuation behaviors. These reconfigured fibers were subsequently subjected to 50 heating-cooling cycles between 70 and 25°C to assess their reversible actuation performance. During each cycle, changes in the axial length of the helix were recorded to quantify actuation strain and evaluate fatigue resistance.

Data availability
The authors declare that the data supporting the findings of this study are provided within the article and its Supplementary Information file. Additional data were available upon request from the corresponding author. Source data are provided with this paper.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
There are two highlights of this work: 1. The fabrication of Janus-structured fibrous artificial muscles by bicomponent extrusion spinning; the combination of polyurethane (PU) and liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) improves the mechanical properties of the LCE. 2. Leveraging the soft elasticity of liquid crystal elastomers and the dynamic bond exchange of polyurethane (PU), multi-modal shape programming of Janus fibers has been achieved. However, as a fibrous artificial muscle, shape change is only one aspect; the actuation properties (strain, stress, energy density, etc.) are even more crucial. The following revisions are suggested:
1. For straight Janus LCE/PU fibers prepared by a continuous extrusion platform, please provide their actuation strain, actuation strain rate, actuation stress, as well as energy density, these metrics are important to evaluate actuation properties for shape-changing materials used as artificial muscles.
2. For spring-like Janus fiber actuators, how about their loading capabilities? Can these spring-like soft actuators load external load and cyclically lift the load like a soft spring upon thermal actuation?
3. What factors influence the order parameter? What is the range of the order parameter for processed fiber?
4. For continuous extrusion-stretching process，Fig. 1c is a schematic diagram of processing device and fiber processing. Is there a video actually shot to show the processing device and the processing process?
5. For the swimming robot shown in Fig. 5b, the authors need to rule out the possibility of the thermal-induced Marangoni effect. This effect can also propel a floating object on the water surface to move.

Recommendation:
Recommend for publication after minor revisions.
Overall Comments:
This manuscript presents a novel approach for the fabrication of Janus Fibers. The authors create continuously extruded Janus fibers created from Liquid Crystalline Elastomer (LCE) and polyurethane (PU). The authors demonstrate improved properties of these Janus fibers through mechanical testing. The authors also demonstrate the creation of several functional examples of Janus fiber including tendril actuation, and programmable coiling behavior. The work is well written, well executed, and has complete and thorough supporting information for claims. The method has potential for improving existing methodologies for Janus fiber production and advances the usefulness of LCE fibers by improving their properties.
Therefore, the reviewer believes it will be of interest to the community of Nature Communications and offers the following
minor comments.
Items to be addressed:
1) The authors claim “synchronization” in photopolymerization kinetics, suggesting that there is a coupling between the

between stimulus parameters (e.g., intensity, wavelength, duration) and the resulting actuation behavior should be

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript presents a strategy for the continuous fabrication of Janus LCE fibers that integrate a stimuli-responsive
LCE network with a dynamically reconfigurable PU network. The authors demonstrate programmable and reprogrammable
actuation, bioinspired design, and scalable integration into functional textiles, representing a notable advance in the field of
soft robotics and adaptive materials.
1.The success of co-extrusion relies on the viscosity matching between the two precursors. Could the authors provide
quantitative data or discussion on how small viscosity deviations affect the interface stability and fiber morphology?
2.The PU component exhibits dynamic covalent bond exchange above 55 °C, while the Tₙᵢ of the LCE is around 67 °C.
Figure 2i indicates that the PU network undergoes relatively fast stress relaxation upon heating. Could the authors elaborate
on how the rate of dynamic bond exchange affects the long-term actuation stability, as well as potential creep and fatigue
behaviors under repeated thermal cycling?
3.Regarding the fabrication process of the Janus fibers, I have several technical questions: (1) The process involves a two-
step UV curing. How is the crosslinking degree controlled during the first UV exposure to ensure that further alignment and
secondary curing can proceed effectively? (2) During the first UV curing, does the partial polymerization already fix the
shear-induced orientation of the LCE domains, or is the alignment mainly achieved during the subsequent stretching step?
(3) Upon the final thermal treatment, will the pre-aligned LCE phase experience slight shrinkage that may influence the
morphology of the adjacent PU domain, even if the temperature does not reach Tₙᵢ? (4) Could the authors further elaborate
on the detailed mechanism by which heating promotes hydrogen-bond formation within the PU network?
4.What is the interfacial adhesion strength between the LCE and PU domains? Are these two materials prone to
delamination under mechanical deformation? For long-term use, could a mismatch in strain or modulus between the LCE
and PU layers lead to interfacial instability or fatigue?
5.In Figure 3c, what is the surface temperature reached during NIR laser irradiation? Is the temperature distribution across
the irradiated region uniform? Typically, the central zone tends to be hotter than the edges—how do the authors ensure
controlled and uniform photothermal processing?
6.Upon localized heating by NIR light, does the LCE layer experience partial thermal transition or contraction that might
introduce internal stresses or deformation gradients within the Janus structure?
7.Does the PU network contain any catalyst that facilitates the dynamic covalent exchange reaction? If not, how can the
urethane bond exchange proceed efficiently at such a relatively low temperature and with a low apparent activation energy?
It is suggested that the authors provide more detailed synthetic procedures of the polymer precursors to minimize confusion.
8.How did the authors regulate the viscosities of the LCE and PU precursors during co-extrusion? Were any solvents used
in the precursor formulations? If solvents were employed, could their evaporation affect the fiber morphology, phase
interface, or mechanical performance during fabrication?

## Abstract

Smart fibers, particularly liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) fibers, are pivotal in soft robotics and adaptive textiles. However, existing fabrication methods are limited to simple monolithic structures, hindering the realization of complex actuation behaviors. To overcome this limitation, we develop a continuous extrusion platform for producing Janus LCE fibers that emulate asymmetric biological structures, such as plant tendrils, thereby enabling sophisticated actuation. This approach seamlessly integrates an LCE network with a dynamic covalent polymer network, allowing programmable on-demand liquid crystal orientation for actuation via dynamic bond exchange. The resulting Janus fibers exhibit enhanced mechanical properties and multifunctional capabilities, including adaptive object manipulation, stimuli-responsive directional motion, and scalable integration into smart fabrics for thermal management. By unifying material intelligence with structural programmability, this work advances the development of bioinspired soft robotic systems with enhanced environmental adaptability.

---

## Introduction

Fibrous artificial muscles 1–6 are crucial for a wide range of applications, including prosthetic limbs 6, adaptive textiles 7–10, and miniature actuators 5, 11–14. Among polymer-based smart fibers (e.g., responsive gels 15, 16, shape-memory polymers 17, 18, dielectric elastomers 19, and thermally expandable polymers), liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) stand out due to their high reversible strain and rapid response 20. Their actuation behavior is determined by two key factors: geometric structure and liquid crystal orientation, where the former dictates their application scenarios and the latter governs their ability to undergo reversible deformation under external stimuli. Building on the seminal study that established the basic principle for producing LCE fibers via mechanical stretching followed by photopolymerization to achieve mesogen alignment 21, several advanced fabrication techniques have emerged. These include melt drawing 22, direct ink writing 23, 24, and electrospinning 25, 26, all proven effective in fabricating LCE fibers with strong actuation properties. Their structures, however, are typically constrained to simple and monolithic forms, which limits the potential for achieving complex actuation behaviors.

In nature, plants like tendrils exhibit sophisticated deformations through asymmetric fiber lignification, forming helical structures that are capable of multimodal bending and coiling, thereby adapting to the environment 27. Mimicking such mechanisms in artificial muscles requires replicating intrinsic structural complexity, yet existing approaches struggle to achieve this. Pioneering work demonstrating “self-winding” LCE utilized a mold-fabricated helical precursor. Locking the orientation during secondary stretching enabled controllable shape transformations, including bending, twisting, coiling, and contraction, within a monolithic fibrous architecture 28. An elegant approach involves leveraging the shear gradient differential between the core and sheath during direct ink writing to program varying liquid crystal orientations in LCE fibers, enabling complex actuation modalities 29. This approach primarily modulates orientation distributions while remaining constrained in terms of hierarchical structural design.

Janus architectures, integrating two distinct materials with different functionalities within a compact structure, offer an innovative paradigm for sophisticated structural and functional design 30–32. Fabricating Janus architectures beyond nanoparticles or thin membranes remains challenging, primarily due to the difficulty in achieving uniform anisotropic construction throughout three-dimensional fibrous structures. Although millimeter-scale Janus hydrogel fibers have been produced via wet spinning 33, these methodologies prove fundamentally incompatible with LCE. This arises from LCEs’ stringent requirements for both liquid crystal phase preservation and precise liquid crystal orientation, a criterion that current hydrogel-based fabrication techniques cannot meet due to inherent chemical constraints. Furthermore, these existing approaches are restricted to producing large-diameter fibers, limiting their applicability. We envision whether we can fabricate a Janus fiber that combines asymmetric structural design with multifunctional performance. The selection of material composition is critical: one component should provide actuation capabilities, while the other serves as a structural support with programmable orientation control. Here, dynamic covalent polymers 34–36, usually copolymerized with LCE, are particularly well-suited for this purpose, as their bond exchange reactions permit the on-demand programming of liquid crystal orientation. Beyond that, dynamic covalent polymers like polyurethane enhance mechanical robustness significantly when incorporated into LCE to form interpenetrating networks, enabling ultrastrong actuation-mechanics properties and representing a milestone in high-performance LCE development 37.

Therefore, we present in this work a continuous asymmetric extrusion platform for the seamless integration of an LCE network (for actuation) with a dynamic covalent polymer network (for programming). The selection of compatible chemistries is critical, as the two polymer precursors must exhibit matched extrusion viscosities, identical curing conditions, and synchronized curing kinetics. Through precise chemical design, we employ UV-curable LCE and the dynamic covalent polymer to enable continuous Janus fiber production. The resulting Janus fibers exhibit adaptive object manipulation, directional motion under thermal/infrared laser stimuli, and navigation capabilities in complex environments. This work merges material intelligence with structural programmability, paving the way for multifunctional soft robots with bioinspired environmental adaptability.

## Results

Bioinspired continuous fabrication of Janus fibers
As Fig. 1a illustrates, plant tendrils usually induce anisotropic contraction through asymmetric lignification of gelatinous fiber (g-fiber) cells, which finally leads to helical coiling to adapt to the environment 27. Such tendrils can be considered as natural Janus structures capable of switching between “on” and “off” states through the modulation of intrinsic curvature 38. This characteristic enables them to be sufficiently compliant for interaction with the environment while remaining mechanically robust enough to perform functional tasks (Fig. 1b). Inspired by this, we design a continuous asymmetric spinning platform to fabricate Janus fibers (Fig. 1c and Movie S1). This platform co-extrudes two precursors through a conical Janus nozzle, followed by an in situ ultraviolet (UV) light curing. These two precursors are composed of LCE and polyurethane (PU) precursors, respectively (Fig. 1d). Specifically, the LCE precursor is synthesized via the thiol-Michael addition reaction among 1,4-bis[4-(6-acryloyloxyhexyloxy)benzoyloxy]-2-methylbenzene (RM82), 3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol (DODT), and pentaerythritol tetrakis(3-mercaptopropionate) (PETMP). The PU precursor is prepared in accordance with the procedure described in the literature 33. The chemical structures of both precursors are characterized by nuclear magnetic resonance, as shown in Fig. S1. Janus fibers that contained these two materials are then partially cured through the photoinitiated free radical polymerization of (meth)acrylate from two precursors.

To further induce mesogens alignment in LCE, the fibers are mechanically drawn using a differential-speed winding system, followed by a secondary UV curing process, which allows the materials to be fully cured to lock the strain-induced orientation. This dual-step curing process separates geometric structure formation from functional orientation fixing, enabling programmable on-demand actuation of LCE. Subsequent thermal annealing facilitates the ordered reorganization of hydrogen bonds through dynamic bond exchange within the PU segments, ultimately strengthening the mechanical integrity of the fibers 35.

The experimental details of the whole process can be found in the Supplementary Information. All processing steps can be conducted under ambient conditions without the need for oxygen degassing. This facilitates greater accessibility and scalability of the process, while ensuring the maintenance of chemical fidelity. Consequently, the Janus fiber obtained through this method exhibit a well-defined biphasic morphology in cross-section at the microscopic level (Fig. 1e) and possess the potential for scalable production at the macroscopic level (Fig. 1f). Compared with conventional LCE fibers reported in the literature 5, 29, 39–52, it demonstrates not only a higher elastic modulus but also greater breaking strength, which can be attributed to the mechanical reinforcement provided by the PU component (Fig. 1g).

The successful continuous fabrication of Janus fibers relies on achieving precise compatibility in both rheological behavior and polymerization kinetics between the LCE and dynamic covalent PU network. Gel permeation chromatography results reveal that they possess the molecular weight of 1.1 × 10^5 and 4.4 × 10^4 g/mol, respectively (Fig. S2). The stable co-extrusion capability can be attributed to the high viscosity (5500 and 2200 Pa·s) and the shear-thinning behavior of both precursors (Fig. 2a and Fig. S3). In contrast, viscosity mismatch or excessively low viscosities disrupt interfacial stability, leading to distorted Janus interfaces or droplet-like co-extrusion morphologies, underscoring the necessity of maintaining an appropriately matched rheological window for continuous fiber formation (Figs. S4 and S5). More importantly, the photopolymerization kinetics of the two precursors exhibit remarkable synchronization. Upon exposure to 365 nm UV light, the LCE precursor undergoes rapid photopolymerization, as evidenced by time-resolved infrared spectroscopy and the corresponding increase in acrylate conversion (Fig. 2b and Fig. S6). According to Flory’s gelation theory, the LCE precursor reaches the gel point after 2 s of exposure (calculations provided in the Supporting Information). Similarly, the PU precursor displays comparably fast crosslinking kinetics, with the gel fraction exceeding >21% within 2 s (Fig. 2c). These rapid curing dynamics enable the concurrent formation of both networks, thereby ensuring fiber solidification during the initial stages of UV curing.

Properties regulation of Janus fibers
The composition and morphology of Janus fibers can be further regulated by adjusting the extrusion speed. As shown in Fig. 2d, when the extrusion speeds of LCE and PU precursor solutions are identical, the diameter of the Janus fibers decreases with increasing extrusion speed. Conversely, when the extrusion speeds differ, the component with the slower extrusion speed exhibits a higher content (Fig. 2e). Hereafter, we use the same extrusion speed of 5 m·min^−1. Longitudinal SEM images confirm the clear two-phase interface along the fiber axis. SEM images of knotted fibers show that the Janus architecture remains intact under complex deformation, demonstrating structural robustness (Fig. S7). Moreover, two materials in Janus fibers remain unchanged when subjected to different imposed twist levels (Fig. S8), confirming interfacial stability under torsion.

The two-step UV curing strategy enables precise control over the crosslinking density to fix the mesogen orientation during fiber stretching (Fig. S9). To evaluate the mesogen alignment in fully UV-cured LCE, polarized optical microscopy (POM) is used to characterize the orientational order of the LCE phase in Janus fibers. When the fiber axis (i.e., mesogen alignment direction) is parallel to the polarizer, the fiber appears dark. When rotated to 45° relative to the polarizer, one half of the fiber became bright, indicating well-aligned LCE mesogens (Fig. 2f). The degree of fiber orientation is determined by the speed ratio of V3 to V2, as illustrated in Fig. 1c. As shown in Fig. S10, a higher speed ratio corresponds to more pronounced birefringence effects. Two-dimensional wide-angle X-ray scattering (2D-WAXS) shows effective mesogen alignment (Fig. 2g), because the initially isotropic diffraction ring becomes anisotropic arcs perpendicular to the alignment direction. Increasing the stretching speed ratio from 1 to 1.8 induces a rise in the orientational order parameter from 0 to 0.61, as calculated from Fig. S11.

Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) identifies two distinct thermal transitions in the Janus fiber. The first corresponds to the glass transition temperature (Tg) of ~17°C, originating from the soft-segment matrix of the LCE network, while the second represents the nematic-to-isotropic transition temperature (TNI) of around 67°C, characteristic of the mesogenic domains within the LCE (Fig. 2h). The PU network exhibits stress relaxation behavior above 55°C, with a faster relaxation rate observed at higher temperatures. This results in an activation energy of ~54.9 kJ·mol^−1, confirming the efficient dynamic exchange of hydrogen bonds in the PU network (Fig. 2i). Beyond that, the resulting Janus fibers demonstrate excellent mechanical performance. As shown in Fig. S12, the fibers exhibit a tensile strain of 156%, a tensile strength of 40.4 MPa, a Young’s modulus of 12.7 MPa, and a toughness of 17.1 MJ·m^−3. Comparison with pure LCE and PU fibers reveals that the Janus architecture significantly enhances breaking strength, effectively overcoming the mechanical limitations of conventional single-network LCE systems (Fig. 2j). This improvement arises from the synergistic integration of the aligned LCE phase and dynamic covalent PU network. A visual demonstration shows that a single Janus fiber (diameter ~200 μm) is capable of supporting a hanging load exceeding 160,000 times its own weight over a vertical distance of ~20 cm during externally driven motion (Fig. S13 and Movie S2), highlighting the exceptional strength and robustness of this hybrid design. To better understand the factors governing mechanical performance, we examined the effect of extrusion speed. Higher extrusion speeds produce thinner fibers, which exhibit increased Young’s modulus and enhanced toughness, revealing a clear dependence of mechanical properties on fiber diameter that can be systematically tuned through the extrusion parameters (Fig. S14). In addition to their improved mechanical robustness, the continuously extruded Janus fibers also display excellent thermal actuation performance. Upon heating, the fibers undergo a transition from a linear to a helical configuration; therefore, the reported actuation strain corresponds to a length-change ratio rather than a conventional uniaxial contraction strain. The effective fiber length in the helical state was measured as illustrated in Fig. S15, and the detailed calculation formula for the actuation strain is provided in the Supporting Information. At 80°C, the fibers exhibit an actuation strain of ~85%, defined here as the length-change ratio, together with a high actuation strain rate of 193%·s^−1, and generate an energy density approaching 50 kJ·m^−3 under a load of 200 kPa (Figs. S15 and S16). Collectively, these mechanical and actuation characteristics indicate the potential applicability of Janus fibers in scalable artificial-muscle systems (see Table S3 for quantitative comparison).

Programmable and reprogrammable actuation of Janus fibers
The inherent soft elasticity of LCE 53 and the dynamic bond exchange in PU enable various programming strategies for shaping and actuating Janus fibers. The first strategy involves direct mechanical stretching (Fig. 3a i). At room temperature, LCE exhibits soft elasticity and retains its stretched shape after the force is removed (Fig. S17). In contrast, PU shows entropic elasticity and returns to its original shape once the force is released. As a result, the Janus fiber can coil due to the asymmetric contraction of the two materials after mechanical programming. Further heating would remove the soft elasticity of LCE, causing the coiling to disappear. Representative images of the process are shown in Fig. S18. The applied strain affects the helical structure of the fiber, with higher strain leading to tighter and denser helices (Fig. 3a ii). The helical density, therefore, increases nonlinearly, approaching ~5 cm^−1 at 100% prestrain, while the coil diameter decreases and plateaus near 0.1 cm at higher strains (Fig. 3a iii). The pitch likewise decreases with strain, stabilizing at ~0.2 cm (Fig. S19).

Another approach is precisely the opposite. At elevated temperatures (90°C), LCE is capable of recovering its original shape after the removal of an external force, whereas PU, due to stress relaxation resulting from dynamic bond exchange, undergoes plastic deformation and fails to recover (Fig. S20). Fibers are stretched to 60% strain and subsequently annealed at 90°C for varying durations (Fig. 3b i). The annealing time affects the helical structure of the fibers, with longer annealing durations leading to tighter and denser helices (Fig. 3b ii). The helical density, therefore, increases nonlinearly with annealing time, approaching ~6.5 cm^−1 after prolonged annealing, while the coil diameter decreases and plateaus near 0.08 cm (Fig. 3b iii). The pitch likewise decreases with annealing time, stabilizing at ~0.15 cm (Fig. S21). In this case, when the fibers cool to room temperature, the reversible actuations occur due to the orientation of LCE, which will be discussed in detail later.

To further quantify this asymmetry, we introduced a geometric model:
L2 - L1 = N · H · (sqrt(π^2 · D^2 + p^2) - sqrt(π^2 · (D - 2d)^2 + p^2)) (1)
Here, L1 and L2 represent the lengths of the PU and LCE domains, respectively; N is the helical density; H is the axial length of the helix; D is the outer diameter of the helix; d is the diameter of the fiber; and p is the helical pitch (Fig. S22). Substituting experimentally measured parameters into the analytical model revealed distinct trends in the domain length differentials. Under direct mechanical stretching, L2 - L1 was positive and increased with applied strain, reaching a maximum at 100% strain. In contrast, thermal annealing yielded a negative L2 - L1, with the absolute value reaching a maximum after 10 min of annealing, which is in good agreement with experimental results. These observations confirm the effectiveness of the analytical framework in capturing the asymmetric strain-induced coiling behavior of Janus LCE fibers.

Further implementation of spatial programming strategies enables heterogeneous actuation within a single Janus fiber (Fig. 3c). Near-infrared (NIR) laser irradiation (808 nm, 2000 mW·cm^−2, 5 min) is selected to achieve this activation. The fiber is first uniformly stretched to 50% strain under controlled external stress and then selectively irradiated. During programming, even when NIR irradiation raises temperatures above the LCE phase transition, contraction-induced stresses in LCE are insufficient to overcome external stretching, while PU undergoes stress relaxation. Upon release of the applied strain, two distinct regions emerged, exhibiting opposite spiral orientations and differing pitches. Importantly, when heated to 70°C, the irradiated regions transformed into helical structures with varying pitches, while the previously unirradiated region returned to a linear configuration. These results showcase the ability of Janus fibers to achieve programmable, on-demand heterogeneity within a structurally continuous architecture.

Dynamic bonds enable efficient reprogramming of liquid crystal mesogen orientation, allowing the desired actuation (Fig. 4a). Unlike conventional methods that incorporate dynamic bonds into the LCE network through copolymerization 29, 54–56, our Janus design retains efficient reorientation while preserving the strong mechanical properties of dynamic covalent polymers. After programming, the loosely coiled helical configurations are capable of reversibly switching between loose and tight helices and exhibit excellent stability during two hundred heating and cooling cycles (Movie S3), and this reversible actuation is maintained even when small external loads are applied (Fig. S23). Finite element analysis (FEA) is utilized to predict this actuation, and the numerical simulations show close agreement with the experimental results (Fig. 4b). More importantly, these structures can be reprogrammed into diverse helical architectures through dynamic bond exchange (Fig. 4c and Movie S4). Cyclic testing demonstrates that the fibers exhibit no signs of actuation fatigue within 200 cycles (Fig. S24). After 200 actuation cycles, the interfaces of Janus fiber remained intact, demonstrating that fibers produced via our fabrication method exhibit excellent structural stability (Fig. S25). Additional FEA simulations of all three helical structures are conducted (Fig. S26), showing excellent agreement with the experimental results. This characteristic enables the potential application of Janus fibers as soft robots.

Multimodal actuation and functional demonstrations of Janus fiber robots
Inspired by the adaptive grasping mechanism of climbing tendrils, our Janus fibers demonstrate the ability to autonomously coil for object manipulation. Upon approaching a heated wire at 90°C, localized heating induces Janus LCE fiber curling, thereby enabling firm grasping and lifting of the wire (Fig. 5a and Movie S5). Despite a cross-sectional diameter of approximately 170 μm, the fibers are capable of lifting loads up to 0.5 g, corresponding to a load-bearing capacity exceeding 20 N/cm^2. Subsequent cooling allows for the controlled release of the wire. This localized heating can also be achieved through NIR laser irradiation, enabling on-demand light-guided locomotion, with the actuation magnitude precisely tunable via the irradiation intensity (Fig. S27). We therefore design a “water strider”, in which four of its legs are composed of Janus fibers coated with carbon nanotubes. NIR laser irradiation (808 nm, 5000 mW·cm^−2, 0.5 s) of the left-side legs causes the fibers to bend. Removing the light triggers shape recovery, reversing the bending for movement in the opposite direction (Fig. 5b and Movie S6). This “water strider” can achieve an initial average speed of 4.7 mm/s (Fig. S28a). In contrast, NIR laser irradiation (808 nm, 5000 mW·cm^−2, 0.5 s) on the right legs can generate a rotational torque, achieving a controllable clockwise rotation of ~14°/s and reaching an angular displacement of 125° within 9 s (Fig. 5c and Fig. S28b). These results demonstrate that multimodal locomotion can be achieved through the integration of Janus LCE fibers with different actuation directions by leveraging localized NIR laser stimuli. Control experiments employing non-actuating PU fibers as locomotive elements exclude thermally induced Marangoni effects. These results confirm that motion originates from programmed NIR-triggered bending of Janus fibers. The asymmetric leg configuration, in which the left legs have opposite LCE-facing orientations while the right legs share the same orientation, allows selective illumination to generate either a net propulsive force for translation or an unbalanced torque for rotation, enabling the robot to switch between straight-line motion and controlled rotation in a programmable manner.

Heterogeneous structural design of Janus LCE fibers can also enable directional locomotion. To achieve this, we design a spring fiber with gradient helical architectures (Fig. S29). Upon insertion into narrow glass tubes and heating to 100°C, asymmetric contraction along the fiber generates axial movement. During the cooling phase to 40°C, shape recovery further enhances the overall movement. Through repeated thermal cycling, an inchworm-like locomotion is achieved (Fig. 5d and Movie S7), with each cycle resulting in ~0.2 mm of forward progression (Fig. S30).

The continuously fabricated fibers can be incorporated into smart fabrics through conventional textile manufacturing techniques. During the weaving process, Janus LCE fibers are integrated as weft threads in a plain weave structure, enabling active functional control while maintaining mechanical integrity. The resulting textiles display a uniform weave free of defects, confirming the fibers’ robustness under the shear and tensile stresses experienced during the weaving process (Fig. 5e). When stretched, the mechanical stretching induces a structural transformation in the Janus LCE fibers, generating coiled architectures that increase fabric porosity and loft density. This geometric reconfiguration significantly enhances thermal insulation performance, as demonstrated in Fig. 5f and Fig. S31. And the mechanically induced thermal insulation enhancement is reversible, as mild heating initiates structural recovery to the original compact form. The highly tunable insulation properties render the material exceptionally suitable for wearable and adaptive thermal management applications.

## Methods

Materials
1,4-Bis [4-(6-acryloyloxyhexyloxy)benzoyloxy]-2-methylbenzene (RM82) was procured from Daken Chemical Company. 3,6-Dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol (DODT, 97%), Tolylene-2,4-diisocyanate (95%) and 2-(tert-butylamino)ethyl methacrylate (98%) was obtained from TCI. Pentaerythritol tetrakis (3-mercaptopropionate) (PETMP, 95%), triethylamine (TEA, 99%), dimethylolbutanoic acid (DMBA, 98%), ditin butyl dilaurate (DBTDL, 95%), and Phenylbis(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl) phosphine oxide (Irgacure 819, 97%) were obtained from Aladdin. Poly(tetrahydrofuran)diol (Mn=1000) was purchased from B&D and vacuum-dried at 100°C before being used. All chemicals were used as received unless otherwise noted.

Synthesis of LC oligomer
RM82 (10.00 g), DODT (2.024 g), TEA (2% of the monomers), and toluene (10.00 g) were added into a 50 mL flask and stirred at 70°C for 24 h. After the reaction, toluene was evaporated at 70°C to yield a white viscous liquid, which was further dried in a 70°C vacuum oven for 24 h. The molecular structure was characterized by 1H-NMR and FTIR analysis (Figs. S1a and S4).

Synthesis of PU precursor
The PU precursor containing dynamic hindered urea bonds and pendant carboxylic acid groups was synthesized via three steps. First, poly(tetrahydrofuran)diol (0.05 mol) and tolylene-2,4-diisocyanate (0.1 mol) were added to a three-necked flask equipped with a mechanical stirrer, followed by the addition of the catalyst DBTDL (0.1 wt% of poly(tetrahydrofuran)diol), and stirred at 50°C for 4 h. Subsequently, dimethylolbutanoic acid (0.033 mol) was added and reacted for 4 h. Finally, 2-(tert-butylamino)ethyl methacrylate (0.033 mol) was introduced and reacted for an additional 4 h using ethylene glycol diacetate as the solvent to control viscosity. The molar ratio of dimethylolbutanoic acid to 2-(tert-butylamino)ethyl methacrylate was maintained at 1:1 to ensure equimolar content of hindered urea bonds and carboxylic acid groups. The chemical structure of the resulting PU precursor was confirmed by 1H NMR analysis (Fig. S1b).

Preparation of LCE precursor
Combine LC oligomer (1.00 g), RM82 (0.50 g), DODT (65.20 mg), PETMP (187.30 mg), and Irgacure 819 (10 mg) in toluene (500 μL) with a magnetic stirrer. Stir the solution at room temperature for 30 min to dissolve. The final precursor was collected as a viscous liquid after evaporating the toluene under vacuum. The precursor was ready for use.

Preparation of PU precursor
The PU precursor was mixed with ethylene glycol diacetate for viscosity control, using a maximum solvent content of 40 wt%, followed by the addition of the Irgacure 819 (3 wt%). The resulting mixture was stored in the dark prior to use.

Fabrication system
Janus fibers were fabricated using a custom-built high-speed extrusion-spinning setup comprising a coaxial fiber extrusion module and a synchronized fiber collection unit. The extrusion module employed a modified direct ink writing printhead from a commercial bioprinter (Regenovo, Bio-Printer SR, China) to simultaneously extrude LCE and PU precursors through a custom-designed Janus nozzle under in situ UV irradiation (365 nm, 9000 mW·cm^−2), thereby forming a single biphasic filament. The extrusion and collection speeds were precisely matched to ensure uniform fiber formation. The fiber diameter and the interfacial ratio between the LCE and PU domains were tuned by adjusting the applied air pressure, nozzle diameter, and roller speed. A differential speed between the two rollers (defined by the ratio of V3 to V2) enabled uniaxial stretching of the extruded fiber and was followed by secondary UV curing (365 nm, 9000 mW·cm^−2, 10 min) to achieve further crosslinking of the Janus architecture and to lock in the aligned mesogen orientation within the LCE domain. Unless otherwise specified, the subsequent Janus fibers were fabricated under optimized conditions with an extrusion speed of 5 m·min^−1 and roller speeds set to V1=V2=2 r·min^−1 and V3=V4=3.6 r·min^−1. The Janus nozzle was independently designed and fabricated via DLP 3D printing with a nozzle diameter of 0.4 mm.

Characterization
NIR laser (808 nm) was generated by a laser source (MDL-H-808-5W, Changchun New Industries Optoelectronics Technology Co., Ltd.). Supporting Information Videos were recorded by a digital camera (Sony, Alpha 7). Surface morphology was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-4800). The 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR) spectra were collected on a Bruker Avance III spectrometer operating at 500 MHz. FTIR spectra were recorded using a VERTEX 70 FTIR spectrometer. Gel permeation chromatography (Waters) was performed using tetrahydrofuran as the mobile phase with a flow rate of 1 mL·min^−1. Rheological measurements were conducted with a rotational rheometer (DHR-2, TA Instruments). The alignment and Janus structure of fibers was observed using polarized optical microscopy (POM, ECLIPSE E600W POL) with crossed polarizers. Two-dimensional wide-angle X-ray scattering (2D-WAXS) patterns and data were gathered utilizing an X-ray diffractometer (XENOCS) at room temperature. Mechanical tensile tests of Janus fibers were carried out on a universal testing machine (Instron 5966) at a stretching rate of 20 mm·min^−1. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) was conducted using a TA Q800 analyzer.

Programming strategy 1: direct mechanical stretching
Janus fibers were programmed by subjecting them to tensile strains ranging from 20 to 100% at a temperature of 25°C, followed by the release of the applied strain. The deformed shape was retained due to the soft elasticity exhibited by LCE. The degree of coiling (N) was quantified as the number of coils per unit fiber length (N=n/H), where “H” denotes the original length of the unprogrammed fiber and “n” is the number of visible coils formed after programming. In addition, the coil diameter and helix pitch was measured to assess the morphological response of the fibers under different programming strains.

Programming strategy 2: thermal annealing
Janus fibers were programmed by applying a tensile strain of 60% at 90°C and subsequently annealed for varying durations (1-10 min) under the same temperature, followed by immediate strain release. The resulting deformed shape was attributed to stress relaxation caused by dynamic bond exchange in PU. The resulting coiled configurations were then evaluated as a function of annealing time, and the coil density (N), coil diameter, and helical pitch were further quantified and compared across different annealing times.

Programming strategy 3: spatial programming
Janus fibers were first stretched to 50% strain at 25°C. Near-infrared (808 nm) laser irradiation (2000 mW·cm^−2, 5 min) was then applied in a spatially selective manner to predefined regions along the fiber. The laser was scanned longitudinally along the fiber axis at a controlled speed to locally activate dynamic covalent bond exchange. No observable contraction was detected during programming, indicating that the non-oriented LCE domains and applied external stress prevented deformation gradients, preserving the programming of the PU phase. Upon releasing the applied strain, the laser-irradiated regions—designated as Programming 2—retained their elongated shape, while the non-irradiated regions (Programming 1) spontaneously relaxed into helical coils. This spatially patterned programming yielded a single fiber comprising both linear and helical segments. When heated to 70°C, the fiber exhibited thermally induced bimodal switching: the initially linear segments (Programming 2) transformed into helices, while the preformed helical segments (Programming 1) relaxed into linear configurations. This dual-mode integration highlights a programmable and reversible strategy for spatially encoded multimodal actuation within a single Janus fiber.

Shape reconfiguration of coiling and reversible actuation performance of Janus fibers
Fibers were twisted to a twist density of 6 turns·cm^−1 and heated to ~90°C to activate dynamic bond exchange while introducing internal stress, followed by cooling to ~25°C under constant tension and subsequent release of the applied stress. The resulting fibers were then immersed in oil baths maintained at ~90°C to induce thermally triggered coiling. Simultaneously, further dynamic bond exchange reconfigured and fixed the transient helical shape into a stable geometry. Notably, by varying the inserted twist densities (e.g., 5, 8, and 10 turns·cm^−1), three additional reconfigured helical architectures were generated, each exhibiting distinct geometries and actuation behaviors. These reconfigured fibers were subsequently subjected to 50 heating-cooling cycles between 70 and 25°C to assess their reversible actuation performance. During each cycle, changes in the axial length of the helix were recorded to quantify actuation strain and evaluate fatigue resistance.

Data availability
The authors declare that the data supporting the findings of this study are provided within the article and its Supplementary Information file. Additional data were available upon request from the corresponding author. Source data are provided with this paper.
